themes.definition: This question investigates how courts, agencies, policymakers, and broader political forces have shaped the evolution from interventionist and structural approaches toward economically grounded competition analysis.

themes.name: Should merger efficiencies offset predicted anticompetitive effects under Section 7 of the Clayton Act?
themes.definition: This question examines how courts and agencies should evaluate, verify, and weigh claimed merger efficiencies against likely effects on prices, quality, innovation, and market structure.

themes.name: Can anticipated entry reliably justify permitting substantial market concentration?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether low entry barriers, prospective entrants, or alternative purchasers provide a sufficiently credible constraint on the power created by a merger.

themes.name: Are traditional merger tools adequate for predicting dynamic competition in innovative markets?
themes.definition: This question asks whether conventional market-definition and concentration analyses can capture future, non-price, technological, and innovation-related effects of mergers.

themes.name: Should vertical restraints be judged by competitive effects rather than categorical legal rules?
themes.definition: This question concerns whether distribution agreements, vertical integration, and other restraints should be condemned or approved according to their demonstrated effects on foreclosure, access, prices, and efficiency.

themes.name: When does vertical integration or tying unlawfully foreclose rivals?
themes.definition: This question investigates when linking access to one product or market with participation in another, or integrating successive stages of production, gives a firm the ability and incentive to exclude competitors.

themes.name: Can intrabrand restraints reduce rivalry while improving broader competition?
themes.definition: This question assesses whether restrictions on competition among distributors of the same brand can generate efficiencies or instead harm interbrand competition, consumers, or market access.

themes.name: How should antitrust distinguish beneficial cooperation from cartelization?
themes.definition: This question asks when collaboration among firms produces legitimate efficiencies and when coordination instead suppresses independent rivalry, raises prices, or facilitates collusion.

themes.name: What is the proper scope of the rule of reason for agreements under Sherman Act Section 1?
themes.definition: This question examines how courts should allocate conduct between per se condemnation, ancillary-restraint analysis, and contextual effects-based review.

themes.name: Should dominant digital platforms be liable for leveraging power from a core market into adjacent markets?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether a platform’s control over intermediation, data, or a core service enables it to exclude rivals or extend monopoly power into related markets.

themes.name: Is platform self-preferencing inherently anticompetitive or dependent on demonstrated market effects?
themes.definition: This question asks whether a platform’s favoritism toward its own products should trigger liability automatically or only when it causes actionable foreclosure, reduced quality, or other competitive harm.

themes.name: Does a platform’s intermediary role shield it from antitrust liability?
themes.definition: This question examines whether acting as a marketplace, information intermediary, or distributor changes the platform’s responsibility for exclusionary or coordinating conduct.

themes.name: Can existing monopolization doctrine address novel exclusionary strategies without new legislation?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether Sherman Act Section 2 can accommodate technologically novel conduct and system-level strategies that disadvantage entry despite the absence of traditional monopoly practices.

themes.name: How should antitrust distinguish superior performance from unlawful acquisition or maintenance of monopoly power?
themes.definition: This question investigates whether a dominant firm’s market share and persistence result from better products and efficiency or from exclusionary conduct that prevents effective competition.

themes.name: Should antitrust impose liability for predatory conduct when conventional proof of intent or causation is unavailable?
themes.definition: This question concerns the evidentiary and administrability requirements for proving predatory pricing, predatory systems rivalry, or other monopolizing conduct under conditions of uncertainty.

themes.name: Are market definition and concentration reliable measures of market power when competition is non-price?
themes.definition: This question assesses whether substitution evidence, market shares, and concentration indices adequately identify power in markets where quality, privacy, innovation, or access matter more than price.

themes.name: How should antitrust evaluate buyer-side market power?
themes.definition: This question examines how monopsony or bargaining power on the purchasing side affects wages, suppliers, output, innovation, and the legal assessment of allegedly anticompetitive conduct.

themes.name: Should antitrust protect consumer welfare exclusively or also address concentrated economic and political power?
themes.definition: This question compares an efficiency- and consumer-welfare objective with approaches that treat decentralization, fairness, individual rights, or political accountability as independent competition-policy goals.

themes.name: Does a narrow, economically permissive antitrust framework produce excessive underenforcement against dominant firms?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether Chicago School reasoning, demanding proof standards, and risk aversion have made enforcement too weak to restrain entrenched market power.

themes.name: How should antitrust balance false positives against false negatives?
themes.definition: This question asks whether enforcement should tolerate greater risk of condemning efficient conduct or instead accept more missed violations, given evidentiary uncertainty and the costs of intervention.

themes.name: Are courts and agencies institutionally capable of applying complex economic standards consistently?
themes.definition: This question examines whether the expertise, resources, evidentiary procedures, and remedial authority of public and private enforcers support reliable effects-based antitrust decisions.

themes.name: How should antitrust coordinate with specialized regulation and overlapping jurisdictions?
themes.definition: This question investigates how federal, state, foreign, and sector-specific legal regimes should reconcile conflicting standards for multinational firms and regulated industries.

themes.name: Should consumer welfare and economic efficiency be the central objectives of antitrust law?
themes.definition: This question examines whether antitrust should prioritize effects on prices, output, quality, and efficiency rather than protecting competitors or pursuing broader social, political, or distributional goals.

themes.name: How much authority should economic theory and empirical evidence have in defining antitrust rules?
themes.definition: This question asks whether antitrust doctrine should be grounded primarily in economic models and evidence or should give greater weight to legal precedent, institutional judgment, history, and normative reasoning.

themes.name: When should horizontal restraints be condemned per se rather than evaluated under the rule of reason?
themes.definition: This question concerns whether agreements among competitors should receive categorical condemnation or individualized, effects-based analysis that considers market conditions and possible benefits.

themes.name: How should antitrust distinguish procompetitive cooperation among rivals from unlawful coordination?
themes.definition: This question examines when collaboration, standard setting, information exchange, or joint activity among horizontal competitors produces legitimate benefits rather than suppressing competition.

themes.name: Should vertical restraints, including resale-price maintenance, be assessed under flexible effects-based standards?
themes.definition: This question asks whether vertical distribution arrangements should be presumptively lawful or unlawful, or instead evaluated case by case for efficiency benefits and foreclosure effects.

themes.name: How should antitrust distinguish efficiency-enhancing vertical integration from exclusionary foreclosure?
themes.definition: This question examines whether integration or vertical restrictions improve production and distribution or instead block rivals and preserve incumbent market power.

themes.name: When does a dominant firm's conduct unlawfully preserve or extend monopoly power?
themes.definition: This question concerns how to distinguish lawful exploitation of superior business performance from exclusionary strategies that erect entry barriers, impair rivals, or leverage power into adjacent markets.

themes.name: Should antitrust address the exercise of existing market power rather than only its acquisition?
themes.definition: This question asks whether possession and use of durable monopoly or oligopoly power should itself trigger intervention even without a recent merger or demonstrably exclusionary act.

themes.name: Do concentration and market-share measures reliably predict competitive harm in mergers and monopolization cases?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether structural indicators such as market shares, concentration, and durable oligopoly adequately capture actual market power and likely competitive effects.

themes.name: Should merger review rely on predicted competitive effects rather than structural presumptions?
themes.definition: This question examines whether merger decisions should be based primarily on economic forecasts and market-specific evidence instead of concentration thresholds and formal market-structure rules.

themes.name: Do merger-related efficiencies outweigh the risks of increased market power?
themes.definition: This question asks when consolidation produces verifiable productive or allocative efficiencies and when those claimed benefits instead conceal higher prices, reduced output, or weakened competition.

themes.name: Can antitrust methods capture non-price harms in digital and other technology-centered markets?
themes.definition: This question examines whether traditional price, output, and market-definition tools adequately measure harms involving quality, privacy, data security, innovation, and zero-price services.

themes.name: How should antitrust assess dominant technology platforms and their use of adjacent-market power?
themes.definition: This question concerns whether digital platforms can leverage control over one market to disadvantage rivals, restrict access, or entrench dominance in related markets.

themes.name: Does market concentration reduce innovation and other forms of non-price competition?
themes.definition: This question tests whether concentrated markets and powerful incumbents diminish innovation, quality, variety, privacy, or other competitive dimensions despite stable or falling prices.

themes.name: How should antitrust balance accurate proof of competitive harm against administrability and overdeterrence?
themes.definition: This question examines whether demanding evidentiary burdens, screening rules, and procedural safeguards prevent justified enforcement or appropriately protect beneficial conduct from mistaken condemnation.

themes.name: Should antitrust intervention be based on demonstrated effects rather than formal classifications or speculative harms?
themes.definition: This question asks whether liability should require substantial market power and likely or observed competitive injury rather than relying on categorical labels, assumed facts, or uncertain possible outcomes.

themes.name: Are conduct remedies adequate for durable market power, or are structural remedies preferable?
themes.definition: This question compares behavioral regulation and litigation with merger control, divestiture, deconcentration, and other ex ante structural interventions against entrenched power.

themes.name: How should courts and agencies divide responsibility for developing economically coherent antitrust policy?
themes.definition: This question examines the relative roles of judicial decision-making, legislative rulemaking, agency enforcement, institutional expertise, and democratic accountability in shaping antitrust doctrine.

themes.name: Can antitrust institutions enforce complex competition rules consistently and predictably?
themes.definition: This question concerns whether courts and agencies possess the expertise, resources, procedures, and clear standards needed to produce coherent outcomes under uncertainty.

themes.name: How should national antitrust systems respond to globalization and cross-border enforcement conflicts?
themes.definition: This question examines extraterritorial jurisdiction, international cooperation, legal harmonization, and the relationship between national competition rules and transnational markets.

themes.name: Should agreements that restrain trade be subject to criminal antitrust liability?
themes.definition: This question examines when coordinated conduct that is treated as a per se violation should warrant criminal punishment rather than civil liability.

themes.name: Should vertical restraints be presumed lawful or evaluated through their market-specific competitive effects?
themes.definition: This question compares categorical treatment of vertical arrangements with economic analysis of their effects on prices, output, rivals, and distribution.

themes.name: How should antitrust law distinguish unlawful horizontal conspiracy from lawful parallel conduct or cooperation?
themes.definition: This question concerns the evidence and economic conditions needed to infer collusion when firms act similarly without explicit proof of an agreement.

themes.name: What economic and legal standards should govern predatory-pricing liability?
themes.definition: This question evaluates when below-cost or strategically low pricing reflects exclusionary intent rather than legitimate price competition.

themes.name: When should exclusionary conduct by a dominant firm be treated as unlawful monopolization rather than efficiency-enhancing competition?
themes.definition: This question asks how market power, business justification, and effects on rivals and competition should determine liability under Section 2.

themes.name: Should tying, bundling, or exclusive customer contracts be condemned when they exclude rivals despite possible efficiencies?
themes.definition: This question examines whether exclusionary effects in these practices outweigh benefits such as lower costs, improved distribution, or product integration.

themes.name: How should merger policy distinguish harmful concentration from mergers that create scale, scope, or organizational efficiencies?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether mergers should be presumed dangerous because of increased concentration or judged by their predicted net competitive effects.

themes.name: Can merger simulation and empirical market-definition methods reliably predict post-merger price and competitive effects?
themes.definition: This question concerns the use of substitution evidence, competitive closeness, and quantitative models to identify relevant markets and forecast merger consequences.

themes.name: Are traditional antitrust standards adequate for digital platforms and zero-price business models?
themes.definition: This question asks whether price-centered, conventional market-power analysis can detect harm in platforms that monetize through data, advertising, ecosystems, or network effects.

themes.name: Should consumer welfare and economic efficiency remain the governing objectives of antitrust?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether antitrust decisions should principally focus on prices, output, and total welfare rather than broader competitive or social objectives.

themes.name: Should antitrust incorporate fairness, distributional, political, or community concerns beyond consumer prices and output?
themes.definition: This question examines whether concentrated corporate power and buyer or seller impacts justify non-economic goals in competition policy.

themes.name: Should firm size, market concentration, or monopoly dominance independently trigger antitrust intervention?
themes.definition: This question compares structural or anti-concentration approaches with requirements to prove conduct-based competitive harm.

themes.name: How should antitrust balance innovation incentives against rivals’ or consumers’ access to essential products, platforms, or technologies?
themes.definition: This question addresses whether intervention designed to preserve access and competition may reduce technological innovation or investment.

themes.name: How much weight should economic theory and empirical evidence receive in defining anticompetitive conduct?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether formal economic models provide reliable guidance or must be supplemented by institutional, legal, and transaction-cost analysis.

themes.name: Should ambiguous restraints be judged by categorical presumptions or by a context-sensitive rule of reason?
themes.definition: This question concerns the choice between bright-line rules, intermediate presumptions, and flexible balancing when conduct has mixed or uncertain effects.

themes.name: How should antitrust decision rules balance false positives, false negatives, enforcement costs, and legal predictability?
themes.definition: This question asks how standards should be designed to avoid condemning efficient conduct without allowing difficult-to-detect anticompetitive behavior to persist.

themes.name: What is the proper institutional division of antitrust authority among courts, agencies, legislatures, and private litigants?
themes.definition: This question examines which institutions are most competent and legitimate to set standards, review mergers, impose remedies, and enforce competition law.

themes.name: Do procedural reforms, evidentiary rules, and enforcement resources improve the accuracy and effectiveness of antitrust enforcement?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether streamlined litigation, clearer burdens of proof, institutional expertise, and better agency capacity produce more reliable outcomes.

themes.name: Should private antitrust suits be screened more strictly when challenged conduct may be efficient or only weakly harmful?
themes.definition: This question concerns whether private enforcement complements public enforcement or creates excessive litigation, deterrence, and liability risks.

themes.name: Can national competition regimes protect domestic interests without distorting competition in interconnected international markets?
themes.definition: This question examines the tension between domestic industrial or trade objectives, cross-border competition, and coordination among overlapping enforcement authorities.

themes.name: Should antitrust liability turn on demonstrated effects on competition rather than formal classifications of business conduct?
themes.definition: This question examines whether courts should evaluate restraints, exclusions, and collaborations by their economic effects instead of categories such as coercion, refusal to deal, or restraint of trade.

themes.name: When should courts use per se condemnation rather than effects-based rule-of-reason analysis?
themes.definition: This question addresses whether practices such as price fixing and vertical restraints can be reliably condemned categorically or require fact-specific economic inquiry.

themes.name: Can rule-of-reason analysis identify anticompetitive restraints without becoming too uncertain or permissive?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether balancing competitive harms and procompetitive justifications produces administrable, predictable, and sufficiently interventionist antitrust decisions.

themes.name: How should antitrust distinguish legitimate competition from exclusionary conduct by a powerful firm?
themes.definition: This question concerns the evidentiary and economic standards for separating vigorous or efficiency-enhancing unilateral conduct from conduct that forecloses rivals.

themes.name: When does disadvantaging a rival constitute harm to competition rather than harm to an individual competitor?
themes.definition: This question examines whether and when lost access, reduced opportunities, or competitive injury to a particular rival implies broader consumer or market harm.

themes.name: When should refusal to deal or denial of access by a powerful firm violate antitrust law?
themes.definition: This question investigates the conditions under which a refusal to supply, share infrastructure, or provide access becomes unlawful exclusion rather than a legitimate business decision.

themes.name: Should vertical restraints be presumed harmful or evaluated according to their effects on competition?
themes.definition: This question addresses the treatment of manufacturer-distributor restraints, tying, vertical integration, and other non-horizontal arrangements under per se or effects-based standards.

themes.name: Do vertical restraints more often correct market failures and improve welfare than facilitate foreclosure?
themes.definition: This question tests whether distribution restraints generate efficiencies such as improved investment and service quality or instead protect market power by excluding rivals.

themes.name: How should antitrust merger policy respond to increasing concentration and market power?
themes.definition: This question examines whether merger review should intervene more aggressively when consolidation raises structural risks even before clear price or output effects appear.

themes.name: Should non-horizontal mergers require predicted price or output effects to be challenged?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether merger intervention may rely on foreclosure, innovation, or structural theories beyond demonstrable short-term price and output changes.

themes.name: How do market concentration, entry barriers, and contestability affect the likelihood of anticompetitive conduct?
themes.definition: This question investigates whether concentrated structures and weak opportunities for entry reliably predict market power and competitive harm.

themes.name: Are traditional market-definition, market-share, and foreclosure tests adequate in complex markets?
themes.definition: This question assesses whether conventional structural indicators understate cumulative, localized, platform-mediated, or otherwise difficult-to-measure competitive effects.

themes.name: Can predatory-pricing rules deter exclusion without chilling aggressive procompetitive pricing?
themes.definition: This question examines whether above-cost and cost-based standards correctly distinguish unlawful sacrifice from legitimate low pricing by an incumbent.

themes.name: How should antitrust account for innovation and dynamic competition without discouraging beneficial conduct?
themes.definition: This question concerns whether existing legal tests can weigh effects on technological change, investment incentives, and future competition alongside present consumer benefits.

themes.name: Are traditional antitrust tools adequate for concentrated power and novel harms in digital or platform-mediated markets?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether court-centered doctrine, market definitions, and remedies can address intermediary power and new forms of online consumer or rival harm.

themes.name: Should antitrust prioritize consumer welfare and economic efficiency over protection of competitors or broader political values?
themes.definition: This question addresses the proper normative objective of antitrust when consumer gains conflict with concerns about fairness, corporate power, social welfare, or political influence.

themes.name: How should antitrust standards balance false positives against false negatives under uncertainty?
themes.definition: This question examines whether enforcement should favor precaution against missed harms or restraint against condemning conduct that improves competition.

themes.name: Does economic theory and empirical evidence improve antitrust decisions, or can it distort legal judgment?
themes.definition: This question evaluates the reliability, predictive adequacy, and legal influence of economic models and evidence in defining markets and assessing competitive effects.

themes.name: How should courts and agencies divide responsibility for translating broad antitrust statutes into workable rules?
themes.definition: This question investigates the institutional allocation of antitrust lawmaking among Congress, courts, administrative agencies, and expert economic decision-makers.

themes.name: Do existing enforcement institutions and remedies effectively deter and redress anticompetitive conduct?
themes.definition: This question examines agency design, resource allocation, public and private enforcement, penalties, behavioral remedies, and coordination among federal, state, and international authorities.

themes.name: Do exclusive dealing, exclusive territories, and similar vertical restraints unlawfully foreclose rivals, or can their efficiencies justify them?
themes.definition: This question concerns when distribution restraints restrict downstream access and competition sufficiently to warrant liability despite possible coordination, investment, or cost-saving benefits.

themes.name: Should acquisitions of nascent or potential competitors receive heightened antitrust scrutiny in concentrated markets?
themes.definition: This question asks whether merger law should block acquisitions that eliminate a future source of rivalry even when the target has limited current sales or market share.

themes.name: Do network effects, switching costs, and platform lock-in allow dominant digital firms to retain market power despite nominally easy entry?
themes.definition: This question examines whether digital-market features prevent entry and user switching from disciplining powerful platforms and intermediaries.

themes.name: How should antitrust law define markets when digital platforms combine products, services, data, or formerly separate offerings?
themes.definition: This question addresses whether conventional product and geographic market definitions accurately capture bundled, multi-sided, and technology-convergent markets.

themes.name: Should market power depend primarily on market share, or on entry conditions, control of bottlenecks, and rivals’ ability to duplicate critical assets?
themes.definition: This question evaluates alternative methods for identifying durable power when conventional concentration measures do not capture access advantages or competitive constraints.

themes.name: Should exclusionary-conduct liability be based on demonstrated competitive effects rather than formal categories or presumptions?
themes.definition: This question asks whether courts should replace rules such as per se treatment and rigid doctrinal categories with fact-specific analysis of actual or probable effects.

themes.name: May a monopolist use power in one market to suppress competition in an adjacent market or control access to consumers?
themes.definition: This question concerns leveraging, cross-market exclusion, and conduct by firms that control an essential distribution, search, information, or intermediary channel.

themes.name: Should antitrust liability recognize reductions in innovation, quality, variety, or consumer choice even without immediate price increases?
themes.definition: This question tests whether price-centered consumer-welfare analysis adequately captures important non-price and long-term competitive harms.

themes.name: How should claimed efficiency gains and cost savings be weighed against foreclosure, concentration, or other competitive harms?
themes.definition: This question concerns the evidentiary and normative standards for accepting efficiencies as defenses to mergers, restraints, pricing practices, or integration.

themes.name: Can antitrust law distinguish lawful parallel pricing and information exchange from collusive coordination among competitors?
themes.definition: This question examines how courts and agencies should infer unlawful agreement when firms behave similarly or coordinate through digital, B2B, or other information systems.

themes.name: Are economic models and empirical evidence sufficiently reliable to support antitrust decisions in complex and assumption-sensitive cases?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether formal economic analysis improves decisions or instead produces uncertain conclusions when evidence about effects and counterfactuals is limited.

themes.name: Should antitrust protect competitive rivalry and decentralized market structures even when intervention may sacrifice some efficiency or short-term consumer benefits?
themes.definition: This question addresses the conflict between structural and rivalry-based goals and an exclusively efficiency- or consumer-welfare-centered approach.

themes.name: Should antitrust’s primary evaluative standard remain consumer welfare measured largely through prices and output?
themes.definition: This question asks whether antitrust should prioritize price effects or incorporate producer interests, competitive opportunities, public values, and broader non-price welfare effects.

themes.name: How should enforcement authority be divided among competition agencies, courts, legislatures, and sector regulators?
themes.definition: This question concerns institutional design, jurisdiction, accountability, transparency, and the allocation of responsibility for competition-law decisions.

themes.name: How far should courts go in developing or reconciling antitrust standards when statutory language and precedent are ambiguous?
themes.definition: This question examines the boundary between legitimate judicial interpretation and judicial lawmaking in unsettled areas of monopolization, restraints, mergers, and remedies.

themes.name: Should antitrust use simple predictable rules or flexible effects-based standards when courts face high error costs and limited information?
themes.definition: This question weighs administrability, consistency, and deterrence against the risk that categorical rules will condemn beneficial conduct or miss sophisticated exclusion.

themes.name: What remedies and sanctions best deter monopoly, cartel, and other antitrust violations without imposing excessive intervention costs?
themes.definition: This question concerns the design of structural, conduct, civil, and criminal remedies and their interaction with deterrence, proportionality, and enforcement error.

themes.name: How should antitrust treat refusal-to-deal, essential-facility access, and exclusion justified by interests outside ordinary competition?
themes.definition: This question asks when a firm or private organization controlling access to a market must share, deal, or provide access despite legitimate property, security, or organizational interests.

themes.name: How should competition law operate at the boundary between antitrust and sector-specific regulation or socially distinctive institutions?
themes.definition: This question examines whether exemptions, regulated-market doctrines, and special institutional contexts should limit ordinary antitrust liability or enforcement.

themes.name: Do divergences among U.S., EU, and other national competition regimes improve or undermine enforcement against cross-border market power?
themes.definition: This question concerns international convergence, extraterritorial enforcement, and whether lessons from foreign approaches can improve domestic competition policy.

themes.name: When should parallel conduct among competitors be treated as evidence of an unlawful agreement under Sherman Act §1?
themes.definition: This question examines how courts can distinguish tacit or indirect collusion from independent, rational, or procompetitive parallel conduct.

themes.name: Which enforcement mechanisms most effectively deter cartel formation and sustain cartel instability?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether public sanctions, private damages, leniency programs, and related enforcement tools successfully prevent and dismantle cartels.

themes.name: Should collaborations among competing firms, including joint ventures and consortia, receive rule-of-reason treatment?
themes.definition: This question assesses when cooperation among rivals promotes innovation or efficiency and when it facilitates coordination or suppresses competition.

themes.name: Do vertical restraints generally promote distribution efficiency or facilitate anticompetitive foreclosure and coordination?
themes.definition: This question evaluates how manufacturer-distributor restraints should be assessed when they may improve product distribution while limiting rival access.

themes.name: Should resale price maintenance remain per se unlawful or instead be evaluated under the rule of reason?
themes.definition: This question concerns whether minimum resale prices are more accurately treated as inherently harmful or as practices whose legality depends on market-specific effects.

themes.name: What legal and economic test best distinguishes lawful competition by a dominant firm from unlawful monopolization?
themes.definition: This question examines how Section 2 should identify exclusionary conduct without penalizing efficient business strategies by firms possessing market power.

themes.name: Under what conditions should predatory pricing be condemned despite the possibility that low prices benefit consumers?
themes.definition: This question evaluates the appropriate relationship among below-cost pricing, recoupment, consumer welfare, and the risk of deterring aggressive price competition.

themes.name: Should a firm be liable for using power in a primary product or platform to exclude rivals in an adjacent market?
themes.definition: This question investigates leveraging, tying, installed-base effects, and control over essential content or technology as sources of cross-market foreclosure.

themes.name: How reliably do market share, concentration, foreclosure, and product-substitution measures establish market power and competitive harm?
themes.definition: This question tests whether structural indicators accurately predict durable dominance and anticompetitive effects rather than merely describing market organization.

themes.name: How should potential entry and incumbent responses affect findings of market power and exclusion?
themes.definition: This question examines whether credible future entry constrains dominant firms and whether conduct that eliminates or deters entrants should be treated as anticompetitive.

themes.name: Can merger review reliably distinguish efficiency-enhancing consolidation from mergers that create durable market power?
themes.definition: This question addresses the evidentiary and predictive difficulties of identifying merger effects, including the risks of both underenforcement and blocking beneficial transactions.

themes.name: Should antitrust law consider harms to suppliers, workers, competitors, or other nontraditional participants in addition to consumer price and output effects?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether competition policy should incorporate monopsony, distributional, and longer-term structural harms beyond conventional consumer-welfare measures.

themes.name: Does antitrust enforcement sufficiently protect innovation, quality, and market development from exclusionary conduct?
themes.definition: This question examines how intervention should balance short-term competitive harms against innovation incentives and the possibility that dominant-firm conduct produces beneficial improvements.

themes.name: How should antitrust treat competition in markets with free products, non-price quality, data, or other digital features?
themes.definition: This question asks whether traditional price-centered analysis can identify competitive harm when products are free or rivalry occurs through quality, privacy, attention, or technology.

themes.name: When should complex restraints be governed by per se rules, presumptions, or a fact-intensive rule of reason?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether categorical rules and burden-shifting presumptions improve administrability or instead condemn conduct without proof of a concrete competitive mechanism.

themes.name: How much economic and industry-specific expertise should courts and juries use when deciding antitrust cases?
themes.definition: This question examines whether judicial institutions can accurately evaluate complex economic evidence and how reliance on models, econometrics, and expert testimony affects legal outcomes.

themes.name: How should antitrust doctrine balance administrable predictability against case-specific analysis of economic effects?
themes.definition: This question concerns whether clearer legal rules reduce uncertainty and enforcement error or sacrifice accuracy in changing and economically complex markets.

themes.name: Do antitrust agencies have the institutional capacity and authority needed to preserve competition in concentrated markets?
themes.definition: This question evaluates how agency resources, enforcement priorities, interagency allocation, and public-versus-private enforcement affect practical competition policy.

themes.name: Are existing antitrust remedies sufficient to deter, compensate, and reverse large-scale exclusionary or online misconduct?
themes.definition: This question assesses whether damages, injunctions, structural relief, and other remedies are calibrated to actual consumer harm and capable of restoring competitive conditions.

themes.name: Should antitrust law pursue objectives beyond consumer welfare, efficiency, and short-term price or output effects?
themes.definition: This question asks whether competition policy should incorporate broader structural, distributive, political, or social goals rather than treating market efficiency as its exclusive criterion.

themes.name: Should antitrust law prioritize consumer welfare and efficiency over limiting concentrated economic power?
themes.definition: This question examines whether antitrust policy should focus primarily on prices, output, innovation, and efficiency or also pursue the broader dispersion of private economic power.

themes.name: Do market concentration and structural indicators reliably establish market power and anticompetitive effects?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether concentration ratios, firm size, and related structural measures are sufficient evidence of harmful market power or must be supplemented by market-specific competitive analysis.

themes.name: Does entry reliably eliminate market power in concentrated markets?
themes.definition: This question asks whether actual or potential entry predictably constrains dominant firms, particularly where entry barriers, network effects, or other market imperfections weaken self-correction.

themes.name: Should antitrust rules replace categorical presumptions with fact-specific rule-of-reason analysis?
themes.definition: This question addresses whether restraints with both potentially harmful and beneficial effects should be assessed through contextual economic balancing rather than per se or formulaic rules.

themes.name: What evidence should establish an agreement or conspiracy under Sherman Act Section 1?
themes.definition: This question concerns how courts should distinguish legally cognizable agreements from independent parallel conduct, especially when direct evidence of coordination is absent.

themes.name: Is tacit or coordinated conduct without an express agreement a substantial competitive danger?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether firms can produce harmful coordination through signaling, information exchange, or conscious parallelism and whether existing antitrust law can address it.

themes.name: Should vertical restraints be evaluated by their economic effects rather than categorical rules?
themes.definition: This question examines whether resale-price maintenance, distribution restrictions, and other buyer-seller agreements should be judged according to their effects on prices, entry, interbrand competition, and consumer welfare.

themes.name: When does a dominant firm's aggressive conduct become unlawful exclusion rather than legitimate competition?
themes.definition: This question asks how antitrust law should distinguish efficiency-enhancing rivalry from conduct that weakens or eliminates competitors and preserves monopoly power.

themes.name: Can a firm unlawfully leverage market power from one market into an adjacent market?
themes.definition: This question examines whether bundling, tying, discrimination, or other conduct can transfer power across related products or markets in a way that harms competition.

themes.name: What legal and economic showing should be required for attempted monopolization under Section 2?
themes.definition: This question addresses how courts should establish dangerous probability of monopolization, specific intent, monopoly power, and exclusionary conduct in attempted-monopolization cases.

themes.name: Are traditional antitrust doctrines adequate for platform-mediated and digitally concentrated markets?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether conventional concepts of market definition, market power, concentration, and competitive harm capture network effects, ecosystem control, and platform intermediation.

themes.name: Does digital-platform concentration justify structural separation or breakup rather than conduct regulation?
themes.definition: This question compares deconcentration and structural remedies with behavioral restrictions as responses to durable market power in technology platforms.

themes.name: How should merger analysis weigh efficiencies against the competitive harm of increased concentration?
themes.definition: This question examines when claimed cost savings, innovation, or quality benefits should offset the risks that a merger will reduce rivalry or facilitate market control.

themes.name: Are conventional merger frameworks adequate when competition is immature, dynamic, or non-price-based?
themes.definition: This question asks whether static market-share and price-based tools can predict harm involving innovation, potential competition, nascent rivals, or uncertain counterfactuals.

themes.name: Should antitrust intervention proceed when empirical evidence of competitive harm is incomplete or uncertain?
themes.definition: This question concerns how enforcement should balance precautionary intervention against the risk of false positives when effects, efficiencies, or market evolution are difficult to predict.

themes.name: Can economic theory provide a sufficient basis for antitrust rules without concrete market evidence?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether abstract models and economic presumptions should control legal analysis or instead be tested against firm behavior, institutional facts, and empirical evidence.

themes.name: How should antitrust doctrine constrain judicial and agency discretion while remaining economically responsive?
themes.definition: This question addresses the tradeoff between clear, administrable presumptions and flexible standards that allow courts and agencies to account for context and changing market conditions.

themes.name: Should courts, specialized agencies, or legislatures have primary responsibility for developing antitrust policy?
themes.definition: This question examines the institutional allocation of authority among judicial common-law development, agency regulation and enforcement, and legislative reform.

themes.name: Do public and private antitrust enforcement mechanisms provide effective and complementary remedies?
themes.definition: This question evaluates how agency actions, private litigation, damages, access rules, and procedural constraints jointly affect detection, accountability, compensation, and deterrence.

themes.name: Do criminal sanctions and other remedy structures deter antitrust violations without imposing excessive enforcement costs?
themes.definition: This question examines whether the design and severity of criminal penalties, civil sanctions, and structural or behavioral remedies improve welfare by deterring misconduct while avoiding overdeterrence.

themes.name: Should horizontal price-fixing and cartel agreements remain subject to categorical condemnation despite claimed efficiencies?
themes.definition: This question examines whether agreements among competitors that raise prices or restrict output should be unlawful per se or evaluated under an effects-based rule that considers possible efficiencies.

themes.name: Can oligopolists produce anticompetitive outcomes without an explicit agreement?
themes.definition: This question asks whether parallel conduct, tacit coordination, or interdependence among firms can justify antitrust liability absent proof of express collusion.

themes.name: Should ambiguous coordination and mixed-purpose business practices be judged under categorical rules or the rule of reason?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether fact-specific effects analysis is superior to presumptions when conduct may both restrict and promote competition.

themes.name: When do vertical restraints such as exclusive dealing, territorial restrictions, and customer restrictions unlawfully foreclose rivals?
themes.definition: This question investigates the market conditions under which vertical contracting excludes competitors rather than producing legitimate distribution or efficiency benefits.

themes.name: Should resale price maintenance be treated as per se unlawful or assessed for competitive effects after Leegin?
themes.definition: This question concerns whether minimum resale-price agreements should receive rule-of-reason treatment or categorical condemnation in light of their possible efficiency and exclusionary effects.

themes.name: Can tying and bundling complementary products be used unlawfully to leverage dominance into adjacent markets?
themes.definition: This question examines when a dominant firm’s combination or conditioning of complementary products harms rivals and reduces competition rather than generating consumer benefits.

themes.name: Does the Brooke Group standard make it too difficult to challenge predatory pricing?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether requiring below-cost pricing and a realistic prospect of recoupment properly distinguishes predation from aggressive but beneficial price competition.

themes.name: How should antitrust distinguish lawful competitive success from exclusionary monopolization?
themes.definition: This question asks whether a dominant firm’s conduct should be condemned when it maintains or expands market power through exclusion rather than through superior efficiency or innovation.

themes.name: Should antitrust address monopoly power itself or only exclusionary conduct used to acquire or maintain it?
themes.definition: This question considers whether concentrated market power is independently problematic or becomes legally relevant only when accompanied by conduct that creates additional competitive harm.

themes.name: Can antitrust protect smaller or potential rivals from incumbent integration before exclusionary harm is fully established?
themes.definition: This question examines whether competition law should intervene against strategies that impair the opportunities of emerging competitors even when current consumer prices or output have not yet worsened.

themes.name: How should merger law evaluate mergers involving differentiated products and possible future competition?
themes.definition: This question concerns whether merger analysis can reliably identify unilateral effects, innovation harms, and the loss of nascent rivalry when products are not close substitutes.

themes.name: Should structural merger presumptions give way to case-specific effects analysis?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether market-share and concentration thresholds adequately predict merger harm or should be replaced by detailed evidence about competitive effects and efficiencies.

themes.name: Do structural or behavioral merger remedies effectively prevent the loss of future competition?
themes.definition: This question asks whether divestitures, conduct restrictions, and other conditions can preserve competition when a merger would otherwise increase concentration or eliminate a potential rival.

themes.name: Are market definition and concentration measures reliable indicators of market power in dynamic or atypical markets?
themes.definition: This question examines whether conventional relevant-market boundaries and concentration metrics misidentify competitive conditions when products, technologies, or substitution patterns change rapidly.

themes.name: Is monopsony power an economically and legally distinct problem from seller-side monopoly power?
themes.definition: This question investigates how firms’ power over suppliers or workers suppresses prices, wages, or output and whether buyer power requires different antitrust tests and remedies.

themes.name: Should consumer-welfare analysis account for harms beyond conventional price increases?
themes.definition: This question considers whether antitrust should recognize effects on quality, access, privacy, output, innovation, distribution, or other dimensions of consumer harm.

themes.name: Should antitrust prioritize consumer welfare and efficiency over fairness, distribution, and political accountability?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether competition policy should pursue aggregate economic benefits exclusively or also address unequal bargaining power, wealth distribution, and social or individual rights.

themes.name: How should antitrust balance innovation incentives against the risk of innovation-reducing concentration and exclusion?
themes.definition: This question asks when intervention protects future innovation and rivalry and when it instead discourages investment, integration, or the development of new business models.

themes.name: Can effects-based economic analysis reliably distinguish procompetitive conduct from anticompetitive conduct?
themes.definition: This question assesses the explanatory and predictive limits of economic models and evidence used to infer market power, efficiencies, exclusion, and competitive harm.

themes.name: Should courts, agencies, or juries have primary responsibility for resolving complex economics-dependent antitrust disputes?
themes.definition: This question examines how institutional expertise, procedural constraints, evidentiary burdens, and judicial review affect the accuracy, legitimacy, and adaptability of antitrust enforcement.

themes.name: Should antitrust law prioritize consumer welfare and efficiency over broader concerns about economic power and distribution?
themes.definition: This question examines whether antitrust objectives should be limited primarily to prices, output, and efficiency or should also include distributional, political, structural, and small-business concerns.

themes.name: Can economic theory and models provide sufficiently reliable foundations for antitrust rules?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether economic theory can generate dependable legal standards despite uncertainty, competing industrial-organization models, and limits on predicting market effects.

themes.name: Should antitrust doctrine replace categorical presumptions with fact-intensive, effects-based analysis?
themes.definition: This question asks whether courts should evaluate actual or likely competitive effects rather than rely on formal classifications, per se rules, or broad presumptions.

themes.name: How should antitrust law balance false positives against false negatives when competitive effects are uncertain?
themes.definition: This question concerns how enforcement should weigh the risk of condemning beneficial conduct against the risk of allowing anticompetitive conduct to escape liability.

themes.name: What evidentiary standards best distinguish legitimate competitive success from unlawful exclusion by dominant firms?
themes.definition: This question examines what proof of market power, intent, foreclosure, causation, and likely effects should be required in monopolization cases.

themes.name: Is monopoly power alone unlawful, or must it be accompanied by exclusionary conduct?
themes.definition: This question addresses whether antitrust liability should attach to durable monopoly or supra-competitive power itself or only to conduct that creates or maintains that power.

themes.name: How should antitrust law address barriers to entry and strategies that entrench dominant firms?
themes.definition: This question examines when conduct that raises rivals’ costs, disadvantages entrants, or reinforces existing market power should be treated as exclusionary.

themes.name: What rule should govern vertical restraints, including vertical price fixing and distribution restrictions?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether vertical restraints should receive categorical condemnation, presumptive treatment, or rule-of-reason analysis based on foreclosure, efficiency, and consumer effects.

themes.name: How should courts distinguish procompetitive vertical integration from anticompetitive foreclosure of downstream rivals?
themes.definition: This question concerns how to assess vertically structured relationships involving distributors or intermediaries when integration may reduce costs but also restrict rivals’ access.

themes.name: When should cooperation and information sharing among competitors be treated as unlawful collusion?
themes.definition: This question asks how antitrust law should distinguish harmful coordination that raises prices or reduces output from information exchange, facility sharing, or cooperation that improves market outcomes.

themes.name: How should courts evaluate horizontal agreements when coordination may increase bargaining power or produce efficiencies?
themes.definition: This question examines the boundary between cartels and potentially legitimate cooperation among rival firms under the Sherman Act.

themes.name: Should tying and bundling be condemned when they lower prices or benefit consumers but may exclude rivals?
themes.definition: This question evaluates how consumer benefits, pricing effects, and exclusionary consequences should be balanced in tying and bundling cases.

themes.name: How should merger review assess lost rivalry and the risk of coordinated effects?
themes.definition: This question concerns whether merger analysis should focus on the disappearance of competition between merging firms and the possibility that the transaction facilitates tacit collusion.

themes.name: Are market concentration and market-share thresholds reliable screens for antitrust intervention?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether structural presumptions based on concentration or shares accurately identify competitive harm in differentiated, dynamic, or interconnected markets.

themes.name: Do concentrated markets and entry barriers create durable consumer harm that market self-correction will not remedy?
themes.definition: This question examines whether persistent monopoly or oligopoly warrants intervention because concentration enables supra-competitive pricing, reduced competition, or entrenched market power.

themes.name: Are traditional antitrust doctrines adequate for technologically transformed and information-intensive markets?
themes.definition: This question asks whether inherited concepts of market power, competition, assets, and harm can address technology-driven markets involving intangible assets, differentiation, and rapid change.

themes.name: How should antitrust weigh innovation and dynamic efficiency against present competitive harm?
themes.definition: This question examines whether enforcement should tolerate current restrictions when they may promote investment, innovation, growth, or future efficiency.

themes.name: Are price and output adequate measures of consumer welfare in modern markets?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether antitrust should also account for non-price dimensions such as access, quality, innovation, distribution, and other forms of competition.

themes.name: How should responsibility be divided among courts, agencies, and sector-specific regulators?
themes.definition: This question concerns institutional coordination among courts, the FTC, the Department of Justice, and specialized regulators, including whether overlapping review produces inconsistent or counterproductive constraints.

themes.name: Are private ex post lawsuits and procedural thresholds adequate mechanisms for enforcing antitrust policy?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether standing, injury, pleading, evidentiary, and judicially developed screening rules promote effective enforcement or improperly prevent meritorious claims.

themes.name: How should antitrust remedies balance effective deterrence against overreach and unintended economic costs?
themes.definition: This question examines whether structural, behavioral, or less restrictive remedies best restore competition while preserving legitimate business incentives and avoiding excessive intervention.

themes.name: Should antitrust replace categorical presumptions with structured, effects-based analysis when conduct may be either procompetitive or anticompetitive?
themes.definition: This question examines whether per se rules and other bright-line presumptions should give way to economically informed, fact-specific rule-of-reason frameworks for complex restraints.

themes.name: How should courts weigh claimed efficiency benefits against anticompetitive effects?
themes.definition: This question asks what evidentiary standards should apply to merger- or restraint-specific efficiencies and whether they must be genuine, verifiable, and unavailable through less restrictive alternatives.

themes.name: Do economic models and evidence reliably predict competitive effects in merger review?
themes.definition: This question evaluates the adequacy of market-share measures, structural indicators, merger simulations, and other economic tools when competitive effects and efficiencies are uncertain.

themes.name: Should concentration or organizational combination create a presumption of anticompetitive harm?
themes.definition: This question tests whether mergers and other forms of consolidation should be treated as presumptively unlawful or instead judged by demonstrated effects on prices, output, coordination, innovation, and entry.

themes.name: How should antitrust law distinguish efficient vertical restraints from exclusionary foreclosure?
themes.definition: This question concerns manufacturer-distributor restrictions, exclusivity, tying, bundling, and contractual integration, focusing on when they improve distribution and when they suppress rival access.

themes.name: Should foreclosure by a dominant firm be judged by market effects rather than by the mere use of exclusivity or contractual restrictions?
themes.definition: This question asks whether liability should depend on the extent and durability of rival foreclosure, market power, entry conditions, and consumer harm rather than on formal classifications of the restraint.

themes.name: What legal test should govern novel or indirect exclusionary conduct under Sherman Act Section 2?
themes.definition: This question addresses how courts should evaluate technologically novel, hybrid, or indirect practices that may weaken rivals but do not fit traditional categories of monopolization.

themes.name: Should monopoly liability require proof of anticompetitive conduct, intent, or fault in addition to monopoly power and harmful effects?
themes.definition: This question examines the evidentiary threshold for attempted or actual monopolization and the role of intent, conduct, causation, and competitive effects in Section 2 cases.

themes.name: Do price-based screens adequately identify predatory or exclusionary pricing by dominant firms?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether cost-based tests and price-effects evidence capture harmful exclusion without deterring low prices, investment, innovation, or vigorous competition.

themes.name: When does market power allow firms to impose unilateral harm on customers, suppliers, or other dependent trading partners?
themes.definition: This question investigates how market structure, lock-in, switching costs, competitive alternatives, and contractual dependence affect the ability of powerful firms to exploit counterparties.

themes.name: Can cooperation and information exchange among competitors facilitate unlawful coordination without explicit communication?
themes.definition: This question concerns horizontal restraints, joint ventures, B2B systems, and indirect collusion, especially the difficulty of proving coordinated effects when firms do not openly agree.

themes.name: Are joint ventures and other collaborations among competing firms more likely to promote efficiency or create durable monopoly power?
themes.definition: This question asks how antitrust rules should distinguish procompetitive coordination from collaborations that facilitate collusion, restrict access, or maintain market power.

themes.name: Does antitrust adequately address buyer-side and employer market power?
themes.definition: This question examines whether existing doctrine captures harm from monopsony, powerful purchasers, employer concentration, and exploitation of suppliers or workers.

themes.name: Can traditional antitrust doctrine effectively regulate digital platforms and multisided network markets?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether conventional market-definition, market-power, output, and consumer-welfare tools capture network effects, data advantages, platform intermediation, and cross-market effects.

themes.name: Does greater platform use or output necessarily indicate improved consumer welfare?
themes.definition: This question challenges whether usage, participation, or apparent output growth can coexist with reduced quality, innovation, choice, privacy, access, or competitive opportunity in networked markets.

themes.name: Should antitrust prioritize consumer welfare and aggregate efficiency over fairness, market openness, and protection of weaker participants?
themes.definition: This question asks whether the proper antitrust objective is limited to measurable economic welfare or should also include distributional, relational, fairness, and openness concerns.

themes.name: How should antitrust enforcement balance false positives, false negatives, and administrative costs?
themes.definition: This question concerns whether uncertainty, limited evidence, litigation costs, and the danger of chilling beneficial conduct justify intervention, nonintervention, or different proof standards.

themes.name: What remedies most effectively restore competition without imposing unnecessary restrictions?
themes.definition: This question evaluates the design, proportionality, deterrent effect, and practical implementation of behavioral, structural, merger-specific, and post-violation remedies.

themes.name: Can private antitrust litigation effectively challenge dominant firms and coordinated conduct?
themes.definition: This question examines whether standing, pleading, proof, procedural doctrines, and damages rules make private enforcement capable of addressing monopolization, collusion, and digital-platform harms.

themes.name: How should antitrust interact with other legal regimes that authorize, regulate, or protect potentially anticompetitive conduct?
themes.definition: This question asks when conduct governed by intellectual-property, sectoral-regulatory, contractual, or other legal frameworks should nevertheless receive antitrust scrutiny.

themes.name: Should antitrust doctrine be updated in light of modern economic research, changing markets, and accumulated enforcement experience?
themes.definition: This question evaluates the continuing authority of historical interpretations, precedent, original meaning, and conservative judicial approaches against newer economic evidence and institutional learning.

themes.name: Are antitrust agencies and courts institutionally capable of applying complex economic standards consistently and predictably?
themes.definition: This question focuses on agency resources, judicial competence, evidentiary reliability, transparency, coordination across governmental levels, and the need for administrable legal rules.

themes.name: Should antitrust liability for restraints of trade be determined by market-specific competitive effects rather than per se rules?
themes.definition: This question examines whether courts should replace categorical condemnation with rule-of-reason or other effects-based analysis grounded in market facts.

themes.name: Can structured presumptions and safe harbors make rule-of-reason analysis more predictable without sacrificing economic accuracy?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether truncated rules, thresholds, and presumptions can reduce uncertainty and administrative costs while distinguishing harmful from lawful conduct.

themes.name: How should antitrust weigh claimed efficiencies against exclusionary or other competitive harms?
themes.definition: This question concerns the evidentiary and legal standards for crediting production, distribution, innovation, or other efficiencies that accompany conduct increasing market power or prices.

themes.name: Should consumer welfare and demonstrated effects take priority over fairness, distributional, or broader social-policy goals in antitrust?
themes.definition: This question tests whether antitrust should focus primarily on prices, output, choice, and competition or also pursue egalitarian, political, environmental, or other non-economic objectives.

themes.name: Do concentration, firm size, and structural indicators reliably establish market power and competitive harm?
themes.definition: This question examines whether market shares, concentration measures, and structural conditions are dependable proxies for durable power or instead produce misleading inferences.

themes.name: How should antitrust distinguish legitimate competition from exclusionary conduct by a dominant firm?
themes.definition: This question addresses the standards for identifying unlawful monopolization while avoiding condemnation of conduct that reflects superior performance or rational business behavior.

themes.name: Can dominant firms use product design, bundling, or tying to foreclose equally efficient rivals without violating antitrust law?
themes.definition: This question evaluates when redesign, bundling, tying, or integration involving a primary product and an adjacent market becomes unlawful exclusion rather than an efficiency-enhancing strategy.

themes.name: When should aggressive or below-cost pricing by a powerful firm be treated as predatory rather than procompetitive?
themes.definition: This question concerns how price-cost evidence, recoupment, market power, and consumer benefits should be used to distinguish predation from beneficial low pricing.

themes.name: Should resale price maintenance be per se illegal or evaluated under a rule-of-reason standard?
themes.definition: This question examines whether vertical price restrictions should be condemned based on their form or assessed through evidence of output, interbrand competition, foreclosure, and efficiency effects.

themes.name: When do vertical restraints or vertical integration harm competition rather than improve distribution and investment incentives?
themes.definition: This question investigates how antitrust should evaluate non-price vertical arrangements by considering foreclosure, coordination, market power, and claimed efficiencies.

themes.name: How should antitrust address refusals to deal, boycotts, and restrictions on rivals' access to essential assets or markets?
themes.definition: This question concerns the conditions under which a firm or group may lawfully withhold access and when such conduct constitutes exclusionary denial of market opportunity.

themes.name: Do network effects, platform intermediation, and technological design create forms of market power inadequately addressed by traditional antitrust doctrine?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether digital-platform dynamics, switching costs, data advantages, and network effects require revised tests for exclusion, dominance, and consumer harm.

themes.name: How should antitrust analyze mergers involving differentiated products and transactions with both beneficial and harmful effects?
themes.definition: This question examines whether merger review can reliably predict unilateral effects, efficiencies, innovation consequences, and post-merger exclusion before a transaction is completed.

themes.name: Should structural merger presumptions substitute for case-specific analysis of competitive effects?
themes.definition: This question tests whether concentration thresholds and other structural shortcuts improve merger enforcement or incorrectly condemn transactions that may enhance competition.

themes.name: How should antitrust allocate enforcement priority between cartel coordination and unilateral exclusion by dominant firms?
themes.definition: This question compares the relative consumer harms, evidentiary difficulties, deterrence benefits, and institutional costs of pursuing explicit collusion versus monopolization.

themes.name: Do leniency and amnesty programs effectively detect and deter cartels?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether immunity incentives generate reliable evidence and destabilize collusion without undermining private enforcement or imposing excessive costs.

themes.name: How should antitrust decisionmakers balance false positives, false negatives, and litigation or administrative costs?
themes.definition: This question concerns the design of legal standards and procedures when intervention may chill efficient conduct but non-intervention may permit durable competitive harm.

themes.name: Are courts or administrative agencies better equipped to conduct the economic analysis required in complex antitrust cases?
themes.definition: This question examines how institutional competence, expertise, appellate review, and agency discretion affect the quality and consistency of antitrust decisions.

themes.name: How should authority be divided between general antitrust institutions and industry-specific regulators?
themes.definition: This question addresses whether jurisdictional allocation and regulatory overlap improve or impair enforcement in sectors with specialized economic and technological conditions.

themes.name: How should antitrust jurisdiction and remedies respond when competitive effects cross national or governmental borders?
themes.definition: This question investigates the appropriate allocation of authority and coordination among distinct antitrust regimes in globally integrated markets.

themes.name: Can economic theories of competition be translated into antitrust rules that are both administrable and economically coherent?
themes.definition: This question examines whether courts and agencies can convert complex economic models into legal standards that are intelligible, predictable, and workable in litigation.

themes.name: Should effects-based, context-sensitive analysis replace categorical antitrust rules in cases involving exclusionary conduct?
themes.definition: This question asks whether liability should depend primarily on demonstrated competitive effects and market context rather than formal classifications or rigid presumptions.

themes.name: When should courts apply per se condemnation rather than the rule of reason to restraints on competition?
themes.definition: This question evaluates how courts should balance the administrability and deterrence benefits of categorical rules against the risk of condemning economically beneficial conduct.

themes.name: Should antitrust law prioritize consumer welfare and economic efficiency over structural, fairness-based, or political objectives?
themes.definition: This question concerns whether antitrust should focus mainly on prices, output, and efficiency or also pursue deconcentration, political equality, and protection of less powerful groups.

themes.name: Do market concentration and dominant market shares reliably indicate monopoly power and anticompetitive effects?
themes.definition: This question tests whether concentration measures and market shares adequately identify market power or must be supplemented by evidence about entry, competitive constraints, and firm behavior.

themes.name: Should antitrust tolerate greater concentration when firms claim efficiency, innovation, or international competitiveness benefits?
themes.definition: This question asks when efficiency and dynamic competitive advantages justify permitting mergers, coordination, or expansion that increase concentration.

themes.name: How should merger enforcement use empirical evidence to predict the competitive effects of consolidation?
themes.definition: This question examines the role of industrial-organization evidence, institutional arrangements, and uncertainty in determining whether mergers are likely to harm or improve competition.

themes.name: Should merger policy intervene ex ante despite the risk of false positives and mistaken predictions?
themes.definition: This question weighs preventive merger control against ex post litigation, focusing on error costs, enforcement uncertainty, and the disruption caused by blocking or restructuring transactions.

themes.name: How should antitrust distinguish aggressive competition by a dominant firm from exclusionary conduct that suppresses rivals?
themes.definition: This question addresses when superior performance, innovation, expansion, or aggressive pricing becomes unlawful foreclosure or the creation of future market power.

themes.name: Can discounts and other pricing practices by dominant firms exclude rivals while benefiting customers in the short run?
themes.definition: This question evaluates how courts should distinguish procompetitive price reductions from pricing strategies that preserve dominance or weaken price competition.

themes.name: Should efficiencies offset likely anticompetitive effects in exclusionary-conduct and vertical-restraint cases?
themes.definition: This question asks how decision-makers should evaluate claimed cost savings, consumer benefits, and dynamic incentives against foreclosure, higher prices, or reduced competition.

themes.name: How should antitrust treat tying and bundling when the same practice can increase efficiency or exclude competitors?
themes.definition: This question examines whether tying and bundling should be assessed through formal categories or through evidence of their competing procompetitive and anticompetitive effects.

themes.name: How should antitrust distinguish procompetitive collaboration from collusive coordination?
themes.definition: This question concerns when cooperation necessary to produce an integrated product or service becomes an agreement that suppresses competition.

themes.name: Can courts distinguish explicit cartel agreements from lawful oligopolistic interdependence and signaling?
themes.definition: This question examines the evidentiary and conceptual basis for identifying unlawful coordination when firms may coordinate through communications, signaling, or mutual adaptation without an explicit agreement.

themes.name: Are traditional concepts of agreement, market power, and concentration adequate for identifying modern anticompetitive conduct?
themes.definition: This question asks whether inherited antitrust categories remain capable of capturing new forms of coordination, exclusion, and market power.

themes.name: How should antitrust regulate digital multi-sided platforms and network-based markets?
themes.definition: This question addresses how agencies and courts should analyze platforms whose competitive effects depend on networks, multiple user groups, data, and rapidly changing business models.

themes.name: Should privacy and personal-data practices count as competitive dimensions in Internet markets?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether reductions in privacy or changes in data practices should be treated as evidence of anticompetitive harm alongside price and output effects.

themes.name: Can dominant technology firms lawfully use power in one market to preserve or extend dominance in adjacent markets?
themes.definition: This question examines leveraging, interoperability, platform access, and other strategies through which technology firms may expand or entrench market power.

themes.name: Are courts institutionally equipped to decide economically complex antitrust disputes, or should specialized agencies play the leading role?
themes.definition: This question compares judicial adjudication with administrative expertise in developing, applying, and revising competition policy under conditions of complexity and uncertainty.

themes.name: Do private antitrust enforcement mechanisms effectively compensate victims and deter anticompetitive conduct?
themes.definition: This question assesses how private litigation, damages rules, standing, evidentiary burdens, and reliance on generalist judges affect enforcement and deterrence.

themes.name: Do antitrust remedies against dominant firms actually restore competition and improve consumer welfare?
themes.definition: This question examines whether structural, behavioral, or other remedies produce the intended competitive benefits without imposing excessive collateral costs.

themes.name: Should consumer welfare and allocative efficiency be antitrust law’s governing objectives, or should it also pursue fairness and limits on private power?
themes.definition: This question examines whether antitrust should displace distributional, egalitarian, competitor-protection, and political objectives with an efficiency- or consumer-welfare-centered standard.

themes.name: Do low prices and short-term consumer benefits adequately capture the competitive harm caused by market power?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether antitrust analysis should recognize non-price harms such as reduced choice, quality, innovation, bargaining power, or long-term competitive opportunities.

themes.name: Should antitrust intervention occur before demonstrable anticompetitive effects appear?
